name: Sønderjysk Kaffepunch
description: The Danish version of the coin test, with schnapps instead of moonshine — and a firm local rule about how many you are allowed.
funFact: Southern Jutland tradition says you drink an odd number and never stop at one — the old joke is that stopping at two leaves you 'walking in circles', so you continue to three.

steps: Put the sugar cubes and a clean coin in the bottom of a coffee cup.
Pour in hot coffee until the coin is just hidden.
Top up with aquavit until the coin reappears.
Stir once and drink hot, while the sugar is still dissolving.

name: Millimallikas
description: 'Jellyfish': a layered shot of sambuca and Irish cream that curdles into tendrils, finished with a dash of something bitter. Looks alive, briefly.
funFact: The curdling is the point: the acid and alcohol in the sambuca destabilise the cream's proteins, and the strands that form are what give the shot its name.

steps: Pour the sambuca into a shot glass.
Drop the Irish cream into the centre slowly so it sinks and spreads into tendrils.
Add two dashes of bitters over the top.
Serve immediately — it only looks right for about a minute.

name: Vana Tallinn Coffee
description: Estonia's rum liqueur stirred into hot coffee with cream on top — citrus, vanilla and cinnamon against a Baltic winter.
funFact: Vana Tallinn has been made since 1960 to a recipe the distillery still does not publish; Estonians add it to coffee, to hot chocolate, and — controversially — to milk.

steps: Pour the Vana Tallinn into a warmed glass mug.
Add the hot coffee and stir once.
Float lightly whipped cream over the back of a spoon.
Do not stir the cream in — drink the coffee through it.
recipe.garnish: Floated cream and a dusting of cinnamon

name: Lonkero
description: Gin and grapefruit soda, invented by the state for the Helsinki Olympics and never given up since. Finland's national long drink.
glassware: Tall glass or straight from the can
funFact: Alko, Finland's alcohol monopoly, created it in 1952 to serve the flood of visitors to the Helsinki Olympics quickly; 'lonkero' means tentacle, from the original nickname 'octopus drink'.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the gin.
Top with cold grapefruit soda.
Stir once and garnish with a grapefruit wedge.

name: Salmiakki Shot
description: Salty liquorice dissolved into vodka until it turns tar-black. Finland's most divisive export, and it divides on the first sip.
funFact: Salmiakki is flavoured with ammonium chloride, which is why it tastes faintly of ammonia to anyone who did not grow up in the Nordics — Finns consider this a feature.

steps: Crush the salmiakki sweets roughly and put them in a sealable jar.
Pour over the vodka and seal.
Shake daily for three to five days until the sweets have fully dissolved and the liquid is black.
Strain if any grit remains, then keep in the freezer.
Serve ice cold in shot glasses.

name: Brennivín og Appelsín
description: Iceland's caraway schnapps lengthened with local orange soda — the mid-winter compromise for people who do not want it neat.
funFact: Brennivín is nicknamed 'svarti dauði' — black death — for its black label, a hangover from the temperance era when Iceland required spirits to be sold in deliberately unappealing packaging.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the very cold Brennivín.
Top with orange soda.
Stir once and serve with an orange wedge.

name: Black Balsam and Blackcurrant
description: Riga's tar-black herbal bitters stirred into hot blackcurrant juice. Medicinal, warming, and the standard Latvian answer to a cold.
funFact: Riga Black Balsam has been made since 1752 from 24 botanicals and is bottled in ceramic; Catherine the Great is said to have recovered from an illness in Riga after drinking it, which the distillery has never stopped mentioning.

steps: Heat the blackcurrant juice until steaming but not boiling.
Pour into a glass mug and stir in the honey if using.
Add the Black Balsam and stir once.
Serve hot with a lemon slice.

name: Riga Black Magic
description: Black Balsam shaken with citrus and apple juice — the modern Riga bar's way of making 24 botanicals approachable.
funFact: Latvia's bar scene spent the 2010s reverse-engineering Black Balsam into something that did not taste like medicine, and apple juice turned out to be the ingredient that finally rounded it off.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a thin apple slice.

name: Karsk
description: Coffee and moonshine, measured by a coin: drop it in the cup, add coffee until it vanishes, add spirit until you see it again.
funFact: The coin trick is a genuine Trøndelag tradition, and the coffee is deliberately brewed weak so that the coin disappears early and the spirit measure ends up generous.

steps: Drop a clean coin into the bottom of a coffee cup.
Pour in weak coffee until the coin just disappears from view.
Add the spirit slowly until the coin becomes visible again.
Stir in sugar if you take it, and drink hot.

name: Glögg
description: Nordic mulled wine with raisins and blanched almonds waiting at the bottom of the cup — you drink it, then eat it with a spoon.
glassware: Small mug or glass with a handle
funFact: Cardamom is the marker that separates Nordic glögg from German Glühwein, and the spoon is not optional — the raisins and almonds are considered part of the serving.

steps: Warm the wine with the sugar, spices and orange peel to about 70°C and hold for 30 minutes; do not boil.
Strain out the whole spices.
Put a spoonful of raisins and almonds into the bottom of each mug.
Add the aquavit to the pot off the heat, then ladle over the raisins and almonds.
Serve hot with a small spoon.
recipe.garnish: Raisins and slivered almonds in the cup

name: Grogg
description: Swedish shorthand for spirit plus mixer, poured strong: whisky or vodka with soda or cola, and no further ceremony.
funFact: The Swedish 'grogg' descends from British naval grog — watered rum named after Admiral Vernon's grogram coat — but travelled north and lost the rum along the way.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the spirit.
Top with cold soda water or cola.
Stir once and serve, with a lemon wedge if using soda.
